name: Protein pancakes — yogurt & protein-drink batter (פנקייקים חלבוניים)

source.author: Ingredient-list screenshot (Hebrew, app-style shopping-list view)
source.notes: A simple protein-pancake batter: high-protein 0%-fat yogurt (Danone PRO-style, 21 g protein/200 g tub) + egg + a splash of vanilla protein drink + vanilla extract, bound with a little white flour and baking powder. The screenshot lists quantities only (no cooking method shown) — makes 10 units, ~36 g each (varies with pan/ladle size). The protein-drink quantity (30 ml / 3 tbsp) is assumed drawn from a standard ~330 ml bottle carrying 25 g protein total, since only the per-bottle total was given, not a concentration — flag if your bottle differs and I'll recalculate. No frying method specified; standard stovetop pancake method assumed in the cooking guide. Estimate.

serving_desc: 1 pancake (~36 g) — size varies with pan/ladle

ingredients.item: vanilla protein drink, 0% fat, no added sugar (25 g protein/bottle)
ingredients.note: amount taken from a bottle, assumed ~330 ml/25 g protein — flag if your bottle differs
a good-quality one, per the source

steps: Whisk the yogurt, egg, protein drink and vanilla extract together until smooth.
Sift in the flour and baking powder; fold in just until combined — don't overmix.
Cook small rounds on a lightly greased nonstick pan over medium-low heat until bubbles form on top, then flip and finish the other side.

batch_totals.note: Whole batch (10 small pancakes). Protein-to-calorie ratio is genuinely strong — the 0%-fat high-protein yogurt is doing most of the work, with the flour kept to a modest 4 tbsp across the whole batch. Very low fat (mostly from the egg) and low fiber, typical of a flour-light protein-pancake batter.

him.verdict: A lean, protein-forward pancake batter — ~10.1 g protein per 100 kcal, among the best ratios in your library, driven by the high-protein 0%-fat yogurt rather than a flour-heavy base. Very low fat and modest carbs per pancake, so a few of these make an efficient high-protein breakfast or snack. The flip side of being this lean is there's essentially no fiber and it's a small, light pancake rather than a filling meal on its own — plan on a stack of several, plus a topping, to make it a real breakfast.
flags: ~10.1 g protein per 100 kcal — excellent ratio, driven by the 0%-fat high-protein yogurt
very low fat (~0.6 g/pancake) and modest carbs
almost no fiber — a light, flour-light batter
small portion per unit (~36 g) — plan for several pancakes per serving
sodium is modest overall but concentrated from the baking powder
suggested_mods: Top with berries or a little nut butter to add fiber and make it a more complete meal
Swap the white flour for whole-spelt or oat flour for some fiber, with minimal taste impact at this small a quantity
Stack 3-4 for a real breakfast portion rather than counting one as a full meal
Confirm your actual protein-drink bottle size/protein content if it differs from the ~330 ml/25 g assumption — it's a small ingredient here so the impact is minor either way

her_preconception.verdict: Good protein from the yogurt and egg, with some choline from the egg — fully cooked, no safety flags. It's not a folate, iron or DHA source on its own, so it's a fine protein-forward breakfast base rather than a prenatal nutrient standout. Pairing with fruit would round it out nicely.
prenatal_highlights: protein from yogurt + egg; some choline (egg)
suggested_mods: Top with berries or sliced fruit for vitamin C and some fiber
Not a micronutrient standout on its own — fine as a regular protein-forward breakfast, not a dish to lean on for her specific priorities

cooking_guide: Whisk the yogurt, egg, protein drink and vanilla extract together first until fully smooth — getting the wet ingredients uniform before adding flour avoids lumps later.
Sift the flour and baking powder in together rather than dumping them straight in — this distributes the leavening evenly so every pancake puffs the same.
Fold just until no dry streaks remain — overmixing develops gluten in the flour and makes the pancakes tougher and less fluffy, even in a small quantity like this.
Let the batter rest 5 minutes before cooking if you have time — it lets the baking powder start working and the flour hydrate, giving a slightly better rise.
Use a lightly greased nonstick pan on MEDIUM-LOW — high-protein batters (lots of yogurt/egg, little flour) brown and scorch faster than a classic flour-heavy pancake batter.
Pour small rounds (these are meant to be bite-sized, ~36 g each) and wait for bubbles to form across the surface before flipping — flipping too early tears a delicate, low-flour batter.
Tip: a few drops of oil or a light spray between batches keeps the pan from building up residue, since there's very little fat in the batter itself to naturally release the pancakes.
